cards.front: Recall a key point about Organisational Structures
cards.back: A hierarchical structure has many layers of management: clear chain of command but slow decision-making and communication can be distorted through layers.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Organisational Structures
cards.back: A flat structure has few management layers: faster communication and decision-making, more responsibility for employees, but managers have wider spans of control (more direct reports).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Organisational Structures
cards.back: Span of control is the number of subordinates a manager directly supervises: narrow span = closer supervision but more management layers; wide span = less supervision, fewer layers.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Organisational Structures
cards.back: Chain of command is the line of authority from top to bottom: in a hierarchy, instructions flow down and reports flow up. Delayering removes middle management layers to speed up communication.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Organisational Structures
cards.back: Centralisation means decisions are made at the top; decentralisation means decisions are delegated to lower levels. Centralisation = consistency; decentralisation = faster, more responsive decisions.

cards.front: What should you know about business exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating organisational structures, use the FID framework: Flexibility (can the business adapt?), Information flow (how fast and accurate is communication?), Decision-making (are decisions timely and appropriate?). Structure should serve strategy, not the other way around.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: A flat organisational structure is always better than a hierarchical one because it gives employees more freedom. Correct: Flat structures work well for small, creative businesses where employees are skilled and self-motivated.
